findings.headline: Pay award costs create further budget pressures: NJC pay award came in at 3.3% vs 3% budgeted (£0.281m shortfall), and teachers' pay faces pressure from potential Welsh Government 3.5% proposal.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget provided for 3% pay award for teachers from September 2026 and 3% for NJC (Green Book) staff from April 2026. The national employers' pay offer for NJC has been agreed at 3.3%. The report estimates 'there will be an in-year shortfall to the budget of around £0.281m that may need to be met from reserves if there is no compensatory grant allocation.' Welsh Government is consulting on a 3.5% teachers' award versus the 3% budgeted. While Welsh Government stated it would provide additional funding, 'updates will be provided in future reports', creating uncertainty.
findings.matters: Pay award slippage creates unbudgeted costs that may require reserve funding. The NJC shortfall is already crystallised at £0.281m; teachers' costs depend on Welsh Government funding confirmation, which is not yet secured.
findings.figures: NJC pay award 3.3% vs 3% budgeted; estimated shortfall £0.281m; teachers' potential award 3.5% vs 3% budgeted
findings.quote: The budget also provides for a 3% pay award for NJC (Green Book) employees from April 2026. The national employers pay offer of an increase of 3.3% has just been agreed. It is estimated that there will be an in-year shortfall to the budget of around £0.281m that may need to be met from reserves if there is no compensatory grant allocation.

findings.headline: School delegated budget reserves are in overall deficit of £4.798m as at March 2026, with 'significant risk' that approved redundancy budgets will be exceeded.
findings.detail: Schools' earmarked reserves show an overall deficit of £4.798m as at 31 March 2026, an adverse movement of £4.199m from March 2025. The council holds a centralised non-delegated exit costs budget to meet voluntary and compulsory redundancy costs in maintained schools. The report states: 'Due to the current level of deficit reserves held by schools, there is a significant risk that the approved budget is exceeded as specific schools work through any required redundancy processes.' This creates contingent liability exposure for the council.
findings.matters: School budget deficits suggest structural underfunding being managed through redundancies. The council faces contingent liability if school exit costs exceed the centralised budget, which appears likely given the scale and rate of deterioration in school reserves.
findings.figures: School deficit reserves £4.798m as at 31 March 2026; adverse movement £4.199m from prior year
findings.quote: In recent years there has been considerable pressure on school delegated budgets with school earmarked reserves held on 31 March 2026 equating to an overall deficit position of (£4.798m), an adverse movement of (£4.199m) from 31 March 2025 (excluding ringfenced HWB reserves). Due to the current level of deficit reserves held by schools, there is a significant risk that the approved budget is exceeded as specific schools work through any required redundancy processes.

findings.headline: A £2m Strategic Transformation Programme cost reduction target is 'currently assumed to be met in full' but detailed business cases are not due until October, creating material unvalidated savings.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes a £2m cost reduction target from the Strategic Transformation Programme, based on 'a combination of existing and new projects planned for commencement in 2026/27 and is currently assumed to be met in full'. However, 'Cabinet approved some new projects in June which are now being progressed to detailed business case stage and are due to be completed in October. This will help provide a more accurate assessment of the likely cost reduction achievable compared with the target.' At Month 4, the council is assuming £2m of savings with no business case evidence.
findings.matters: Unvalidated savings of this scale represent a material risk to delivery. If these do not materialise, they will compound the existing £7.090m deficit. Deferring business case completion until October leaves two-thirds of the financial year already elapsed with no clarity on achievability.
findings.figures: £2m transformation cost reduction target; business cases due October 2026; currently 'assumed to be met in full'
findings.quote: A cost reduction target of £2m has been included in the budget which was based on a combination of existing and new projects planned for commencement in 2026/27 and is currently assumed to be met in full. Cabinet approved some new projects in June which are now being progressed to detailed business case stage and are due to be completed in October. This will help provide a more accurate assessment of the likely cost reduction achievable compared with the target.

findings.headline: Holiday pay employment tribunal claims (Brazel case) total 300+ live cases with explicit warning that final cost may be 'considerably more' than the £0.254m held in reserves.
findings.detail: Following the Supreme Court's July 2022 judgment in Harpur Trust v Brazel, holiday pay calculations for term-time and irregular-hours workers must be recalculated. Flintshire has 300+ live employment tribunal claims resulting from this. A preliminary hearing was held 5 March 2026, with case management orders through January 2027. Critically: 'There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.' This is an unquantified contingent liability with explicit acknowledgement that the reserve is likely insufficient.
findings.matters: A contingent liability with unknown scale, and explicit warning that actual cost may substantially exceed the reserve, represents material financial risk. If final costs are multiples of the reserve, this would require additional funding and further reserve or borrowing impact.
findings.figures: 300+ live employment tribunal claims; £0.254m held in reserves; risk cost is 'considerably more' than reserve
findings.quote: The Supreme Court upheld the EAT judgment in the Brazel case in July 2022 which impacts on the calculation of holiday pay for employees who work irregular hours or for part of the year (i.e. term time). There are currently 300+ live employment claims progressing through the employment tribunal... There is a risk that the final cost may be considerably more than the £0.254m currently held in reserves for this purpose.

findings.headline: A potential waste recycling infraction fine of £1,022,386 hangs over the council if it does not meet the 70% statutory target; officers meet Welsh Government in September 2026 to determine whether it will be imposed.
findings.detail: Flintshire did not meet the statutory 70% recycling target in 2024/25. Welsh Government confirmed that previous potential infraction charges of £1.203m (for 2021/22-2023/24) have been waived, but stated 'the authority did not meet the increased statutory recycling target of 70% in 2024/25, which means that a further infraction fine of £1,022,386 could be levied'. Officers are meeting with the Welsh Government Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability in September 2026 to 'discuss the progress the authority has made to meeting the statutory target which will assist with determining the levying of the infraction charge.'
findings.matters: An infraction fine of over £1m represents a material contingent liability that could be imposed by Welsh Government and is outside the council's control. This is unbudgeted and unprovisioned, and if imposed would require further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Potential infraction fine £1,022,386; previous waived charges £1.203m; decision pending September 2026 meeting
findings.quote: However, the authority did not meet the increased statutory recycling target of 70% in 2024/25, which means that a further infraction fine of £1,022,386 could be levied and the authority will need to continue to demonstrate a robust and credible plan to achieving 70%. Officers are to meet with the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability in September 2026 to discuss the progress the authority has made to meeting the statutory target which will assist with determining the levying of the infraction charge.

findings.headline: Streetscene & Transportation is £1.739m over budget, with waste disposal cost inflation (£0.520m) and failed income targets (£0.485m) as primary drivers.
findings.detail: Streetscene overspend of £1.739m is driven by waste disposal cost inflation of £0.520m ('increased costs for the disposal of wood and hazardous waste, an increase in bulky waste disposal costs of £0.057m and £0.050m for residual waste tonnage'), HRC trade waste income shortfall £0.200m due to 'lack of take-up from businesses', and DIY household waste income shortfall £0.285m following a member decision not to fully implement proposed charges ('only £0.013m was achieved last year'). The report notes 'brokerage and re-procurement plans will be progressed in all cases to determine whether these costs can be mitigated' but provides no certainty of recovery.
findings.matters: Waste disposal cost inflation and recycling market volatility are external pressures that councils cannot control. Combined with the council's acknowledged inability to raise income through charges, this signals structural cost pressures that will recur unless waste strategy changes.
findings.figures: £1.739m overspend; waste disposal inflation £0.520m; HRC trade waste shortfall £0.200m; DIY waste shortfall £0.285m
findings.quote: There is a projected overspend of £0.520m due to the recent increase in costs for the disposal of wood and hazardous waste, an increase in bulky waste disposal costs of £0.057m and £0.050m for residual waste tonnage. There is a projected shortfall of £0.200m for Household Recycling Centre (HRC) trade waste income due to lack of take-up from businesses and a further £0.285m shortfall for the underachievement of the DIY household waste income target following a the previous member decision not to fully implement the proposed charging for DIY waste.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection is running 0.4% behind prior year (37.6% vs 38.0%), attributed to new recovery regulations and staff vacancies creating a secondary income risk.
findings.detail: Collection rates for 2026/27 at end of July are 37.6% versus 38.0% in the prior year. The report attributes this to 'effects of new regulations governing recovery action and because the recovery process has an extended period before the council is permitted to take court action'. Additionally, 'the service is currently operating with several vacancies, which has placed further pressure on recovery activity'. The council states it will 'continue to be monitored closely throughout the financial year' but provides no mitigation plan.
findings.matters: A slip in collection that is attributed to staffing gaps and process delays, rather than taxpayer default, signals operational weakness. If this rate persists, it could create a material income shortfall beyond current monitoring, compounding existing pressures.
findings.figures: 37.6% collected by end July 2026/27 vs 38.0% prior year; 0.4% shortfall
findings.quote: Council tax collection rates for 2026/27 are currently 0.4% lower than the equivalent point last year (collections at the end of July are 37.6% compared to 38.0% in the previous year). This is primarily due to effects of new regulations governing recovery action and because the recovery process has an extended period before the council is permitted to take court action. In addition, the service is currently operating with several vacancies, which has placed further pressure on recovery activity.

findings.headline: Out of County Placements are £1.685m over budget with explicit warning of 'significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase during the year' due to new high-cost placements.
findings.detail: Out-of-county placements for looked-after children and vulnerable adults are projecting £1.685m overspend. Critically, the report states 'the projected overspend is based on the current caseload of placements and excludes any contingency for net new placements. Therefore, there is a significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase during the year.' This warning comes despite £2m additional contingency already being included in the 2026/27 budget. The council notes 'additional investment has already been made to further develop in-house provision to help to mitigate against such financial pressures', but this has not been sufficient.
findings.matters: Out-of-county placements are high-cost, volatile and demand-driven. A £1.685m overspend on a budget that already included £2m contingency, with explicit warning of further risk, signals the council has lost control of this cost driver and faces ongoing exposure.
findings.figures: £1.685m overspend; £2m contingency already included in 2026/27 budget; projections exclude new placements
findings.quote: Several new high-cost placements have been added to the current cohort in the early part of the financial year causing projected expenditure to exceed the approved budget. The projected overspend is based on the current caseload of placements and excludes any contingency for net new placements. Therefore, there is a significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase during the year.

findings.headline: Social Services is overspending by £4.390m, driven by demand pressures in adult care packages, children's services agency costs and mental health placements.
findings.detail: Social Services accounts for £4.390m of the £7.090m total deficit. Main drivers include Learning Disability care packages £2.194m overspend, children's services professional support (agency staff for safeguarding) £0.772m overspend, Physical Disability care packages £0.520m overspend, and mental health residential placements £0.437m overspend. Additionally, homecare demand including reablement and hospital-minimisation costs is £1.278m over budget. The report notes 'the relevant service areas continue to do everything possible to manage this risk and mitigate this financial pressure', implying these are structural demand pressures not easily resolved in-year.
findings.matters: Social care demand pressures that exceed budget by this scale represent structural challenges, not controllable variances. They signal rising need, rising unit costs, or both, and are difficult to reverse mid-year without service cuts.
findings.figures: Social Services total overspend £4.390m; Learning Disability £2.194m; Professional support (agency) £0.772m; Physical Disability £0.520m; Mental health placements £0.437m; additional homecare £1.278m
findings.quote: The costs of care packages for independently provided services for the Learning Disability service are resulting in an overspend of £2.194m which includes care provision through direct payments, supported living and residential services. The Physical Disability and Sensory Impairment (PDSI) service is also projecting an overspend of £0.520m due to increased net costs of care packages.

findings.headline: Projected unearmarked reserves will fall from £18.261m opening balance to £11.172m, a 39% depletion driven by the operating deficit.
findings.detail: The council opened 2026/27 with unearmarked reserves of £18.261m comprising base level £8.985m, contingency £5.072m, budget risk reserve £2.704m and £1.500m budgeted contribution. The projected overspend will reduce this to £11.172m (base level £8.985m plus contingency £2.187m). This represents near-40% reduction in discretionary reserve headroom. The council states it 'will have a significantly reduced level of unearmarked reserves to deal with any significant in-year unforeseen events' and flags 'several risks identified in the report that could further worsen the Council's financial position.'
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer against shocks. A 40% depletion in one year, driven by uncontrolled deficit, leaves the council with limited capacity to absorb further adverse variances or unexpected costs. This reduces financial resilience and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Opening unearmarked reserves £18.261m; projected closing £11.172m; depletion £7.089m; base level held at £8.985m
findings.quote: Taking all the above into account provides a total opening unearmarked reserves balance of £18.261m. The impact of the current projected overspend would reduce overall unearmarked reserves to £11.172m... Based on current projections the Council will have a significantly reduced level of unearmarked reserves of £11.172m to deal with any significant in-year unforeseen events.

findings.headline: Flintshire is projecting a £7.090m operating deficit for 2026/27, reducing to £4.386m after utilising the remaining budget risk reserve.
findings.detail: The council's projected year-end position shows an operating deficit of £7.090m. After full utilisation of the £2.704m budget risk reserve, this reduces to £4.386m. The projected contingency reserve balance as at 31 March 2027 will be £2.187m. The council explicitly states this is 'clearly of significant concern and needs to be addressed urgently to bring expenditure back in line with the approved budget.'
findings.matters: A deficit of this scale, even after reserve use, means the council is unable to balance its budget from core resources and must deplete reserves. This constrains financial flexibility and raises questions about service and borrowing sustainability.
findings.figures: £7.090m operating deficit; £4.386m after reserve utilisation; projected contingency reserve £2.187m at 31 March 2027; total budget £421.860m
findings.quote: An operating deficit of £7.090m (this reduces to £4.386 with the full utilisation of the remaining £2.704m budget risk reserve). This projected overspend (and impact on our available reserves) is clearly of significant concern and needs to be addressed urgently to bring expenditure back in line with the approved budget.

findings.headline: Council is actively managing down agricultural property portfolio and reviewing industrial units despite fair value of investment property holdings rising to £31.2m.
findings.detail: The council holds investment properties (agricultural and industrial units) classified as legacy assets. Although fair value increased from £29.3m to £31.2m year-on-year, the council is deliberately reducing its agricultural portfolio and reviewing its position on industrial units, suggesting strategic exit from commercial property ownership.
findings.matters: The council is reducing reliance on commercial property income, suggesting this revenue stream will decline as assets are disposed. Any planned property sales should be monitored for their impact on the revenue budget given current dependence on investment income.
findings.figures: Fair value of investment properties £31.2m (2026) vs £29.3m (2025); net investment income from properties contributes to 0.43% of revenue budget.
findings.quote: Although these are classified as investment properties, they are legacy assets, and the Council is managing down its agricultural portfolio and is reviewing its position regarding industrial units.

findings.headline: Strategic Housing and Regeneration Programme (SHARP) commits to building 500 new homes over 5 years with £38m lending limit to wholly owned companies.
findings.detail: The council is pursuing an ambitious house-building programme delivering 500 homes across multiple sites in Flint, Penyffordd, Dobshill, Bryn-y-Baal, Northop and Saltney. New affordable homes are built or purchased by the council's subsidiary NEW Homes, funded by council loans. The council has set a £38m cash limit on lending to wholly owned companies for this purpose.
findings.matters: This is a material multi-year capital commitment concentrating risk in residential property and reliant on NEW Homes' ability to operate and generate returns to service the council's lending.
findings.figures: 500 new homes over 5 years; £38m cash limit for wholly owned company lending.
findings.quote: Over a 5-year period 500 new homes will be built at a range of sites across the county, a mixture of new council houses and affordable homes, alongside commissioning a range of linked regeneration initiatives and community benefits.

findings.headline: Council relies on investment income of £1.69m (0.43% of net revenue budget) including approximately 0.25% margin charged to NEW Homes subsidiary to help achieve balanced budget.
findings.detail: Investment income comprises both a margin charged to the council's wholly owned housing subsidiary NEW Homes and returns from investment properties. The council states this income 'makes a very small contribution to achieving a balanced revenue budget' of £396.657m, representing just 0.43% of total revenue spend.
findings.matters: The council is dependent on investment returns to close its revenue budget. This is vulnerable to changes in PWLB borrowing costs (affecting the margin charged) or volatility in property rental income, both of which could create budget pressure.
findings.figures: Net Investment income £1.69m out of Net Revenue Budget £396.657m; proportion 0.43%; margin on NEW Homes lending approximately 0.25%.
findings.quote: The income makes a very small contribution to achieving a balanced revenue budget.

findings.headline: Lender Option Borrower Option loans totalling £18.95m have call dates within the next 12 months, with council prepared to repay if lender exercises option.
findings.detail: The council holds £18.95m of LOBO loans where the lender can propose a rate increase at call dates and the borrower can repay at par instead. Semi-annual call dates occurred during 2025/26 but were not exercised. However, further call dates exist within the next 12 months. The council has stated it will repay any calls by drawing on available cash or borrowing from other local authorities or PWLB.
findings.matters: LOBO calls are refinancing events requiring either cash reserves or access to alternative borrowing. This represents near-term liquidity exposure for the lender to monitor.
findings.figures: £18.95m of LOBO loans; call dates within next 12 months.
findings.quote: The LOBO loans also have call dates within the next 12 months. The Council has liaised with treasury management advisors Arlingclose over the likelihood of the options being exercised. If the option is exercised and an increased rate proposed, the Council plans to repay the loan at no additional cost as accepting the revised terms would mean it would still have refinancing risk in later years.

findings.headline: The council has allocated £2.704m to a Budget Risk Reserve, alongside a contingency reserve of £2.187m.
findings.detail: Flintshire's reserve position for 2026/27 comprises £2.187m of contingency reserve and a separate £2.704m Budget Risk Reserve. The creation of a dedicated budget risk reserve indicates the council has identified significant budget risks warranting additional protection beyond ordinary contingency provisions.
findings.matters: A material budget risk reserve signals the council anticipates material financial pressures; a lender should understand what risks are driving this allocation.
findings.figures: Budget Risk Reserve £2.704m; Contingency Reserve £2.187m
findings.quote: Less - Budget Risk Reserve (2.704)

findings.headline: Children's Services legal costs of £0.142m remain pending, with final costs awaiting confirmation.
findings.detail: The council has allocated £0.142m for ongoing Children's Services legal matters but explicitly states this is 'awaiting confirmation of final costs', meaning the full liability is not yet quantified. If actual settlement costs exceed this provision, the council will need to use additional reserves to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: Unquantified liabilities create balance-sheet uncertainty; a lender needs to know whether reserves are adequate if these costs escalate.
findings.quote: Children's Services Legal Costs (awaiting confirmation of final costs) (0.142)

findings.headline: £2.0m Strategic Transformation Programme marked Open and dependent on high-assumption confidence
findings.detail: The council's largest single savings item is a Strategic Transformation Programme worth £2.0m, representing 18% of total planned reductions. It is marked as Open (not yet closed) and its achievement is based on high assumptions rather than confirmed figures. However, the council is still projecting full delivery of this saving.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council's major savings initiatives are confirmed or dependent on optimistic assumptions; a material portion of the savings plan carries execution risk.
findings.figures: Strategic Transformation Programme £2.0m target and £2.0m projected (marked Open, High Assumption confidence)
findings.quote: 5 Strategic Transformation Programme Cost Reduction Council Wide Gary Ferguson 2.000 2.000 0.000 O R

findings.headline: Agency staffing costs offsetting projected vacancy savings in repairs and landlord services
findings.detail: Projected vacancy savings are being significantly offset by agency staffing costs, suggesting challenges in filling permanent positions. Repairs & Maintenance sees £0.575m vacancy savings offset by £0.402m agency costs; Landlord Services £0.120m savings offset by £0.154m agency costs.
findings.matters: Agency staffing indicates the council cannot fill permanent posts and is paying premium rates for temporary staff, signalling labour market pressure or recruitment difficulties
findings.figures: £0.575m vacancy savings offset by £0.402m agency costs in Repairs & Maintenance; £0.120m offset by £0.154m in Landlord Services
findings.quote: Projected vacancy savings of approximately (£0.575m) which is offset by agency costs of £0.402m.

findings.headline: Void properties creating £0.621m income pressure on the HRA
findings.detail: Housing vacancy across the council's stock is creating significant rental income pressure through void rent loss, council tax charges, and service charges. The net pressure from voids is £0.621m, representing the majority of the HRA's £0.633m total income variance.
findings.matters: Voids reduce the rental revenue base that funds the HRA, affecting the council's ability to service housing debt and maintain stock investment
findings.figures: £0.621m void pressure; £0.633m total income variance
findings.quote: There is a net pressure relating to void properties of £0.621m. This relates to costs such as void rent loss, council tax charges and service charges and is net of additional income relating to new build properties and voids moving to target rent.

findings.headline: Council's homelessness spending model relies heavily on expensive hotel accommodation; cost-reduction plan depends on housing supply
findings.detail: The review found the council is meeting statutory duties but that "Spending on homelessness duties is not always delivering value for money," with reliance on "expensive and unsuitable hotel accommodation, often outside Flintshire." The council has completed cost-benefit analysis supporting diversification away from hotels with "Projected efficiencies over five years," but full implementation faces a "significant shortage of one-bedroom social housing, particularly for single individuals and childless couples under 50."
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory spend area; realizing projected multi-year savings requires resolution of housing supply constraints, creating execution risk on the efficiency plan
findings.figures: Five-year efficiency projection period; specific cost savings amount not stated
findings.quote: Cost-benefit analysis reports were considered for diversifying homeless accommodation, including moving away from hotels and B&Bs. Projected efficiencies over five years support additional recruitment and actions to further support this diversification.

findings.headline: New Homelessness & Social Housing Allocation Act 2026 will increase statutory duties; council requires additional resources
findings.detail: The Senedd approved the Homelessness & Social Housing Allocation Act 2026, which expands councils' homelessness responsibilities to "more people, at an early stage, and over longer period of time." Flintshire states it "will require increased resources including funding and staffing to fulfil its new duties under the Act," but the paper does not confirm these resources are secured.
findings.matters: New statutory spending obligations represent material budget pressures; if funding is not identified, this creates a structural deficit risk in a statutory service area
findings.figures: Not specified; scope of cost impact not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: The FCC will require increased resources including funding and staffing to fulfil its new duties under the Act.

findings.headline: Multiple RED-rated care cost control initiatives suggest delivery difficulty and rising social care spend
findings.detail: Several items in the social services action plan are marked RED, including respite provision reductions and cost recovery for Supported Living rates (marked Amber with £0.150m target). The respite offer reduction specifically targets only supporting cases with 'imminent risk of carer break down', indicating a shift to crisis-driven rather than preventative support.
findings.matters: RED ratings indicate high delivery risk on planned savings. If these do not land, the council faces social care cost pressure, a typical driver of council financial distress.
findings.figures: Social Services total savings target £0.950m across 5 initiatives; multiple marked Amber/Red
findings.quote: Reduce our respite offer to only support where there is imminent risk of carer break down - marked Red

findings.headline: Civil Parking Enforcement team operating at 67% capacity; income collection at risk
findings.detail: The Civil Parking Enforcement team is understaffed at only 6 full-time equivalents of a budgeted 9 FTE. This limits the council's ability to generate income from parking enforcement, with recruitment ongoing. The £0.020m income recovery target is marked RED as dependent on full team capacity.
findings.matters: Staffing gaps reduce the council's actual income-generating capacity; if recruitment fails, the £0.020m target is unachievable, creating pressure elsewhere.
findings.figures: 6 FTE in post out of 9 FTE budgeted; £0.020m income recovery target
findings.quote: Currently, the enforcement team is not operating at full capacity and only 6 FTE in post (out of a team of 9 FTE). Recruitment is ongoing.

findings.headline: Joint funded social care packages marked RED; council cannot confirm partners are paying their share
findings.detail: A £0.100m cost avoidance initiative targets ensuring joint funded care packages are being correctly funded by partner organisations, with an October deadline. This is marked RED, indicating delivery risk and suggesting the council does not currently have assurance that partners are meeting their funding obligations.
findings.matters: Shared-cost care arrangements are a common risk area; if partners under-fund, the council absorbs the costs. The RED rating suggests this is a material exposure.
findings.figures: £0.100m exposure
findings.quote: To ensure joint funded care packages are being correctly funded by partner organisations - marked Red

findings.headline: £0.200m winter maintenance pressure forecast, uncontrollable and outside budget scope
findings.detail: The paper identifies a potential £0.200m cost pressure for winter maintenance due to adverse weather over the 2026/27 season. This is marked RED as it depends on weather and road surface temperatures that are outside the council's control, though it will be monitored month-by-month.
findings.matters: This is a forecasted pressure that reduces the council's financial flexibility; if weather is severe, it will drive additional spending and potentially require reserve release.
findings.figures: Potential pressure of up to £0.200m
findings.quote: A potential pressure of £0.200m has been forecasted; however, this could be reduced and reintroduced as we proceed into the winter season month-by-month depending on the actual weather. The cost reduction is dependent on weather and road surface temperatures over this winter season, which is outside our control.

findings.headline: £0.737m waste grant funding at risk if Welsh Government cuts support mid-year
findings.detail: The council is awaiting written confirmation of a Welsh Government Sustainable Waste Management Grant for 2025/26, which has only been verbally confirmed. The budget assumes this £0.737m grant will be received, but the paper identifies concern that WG may reduce or remove it due to DEFRA central funding pressures.
findings.matters: This is a material mid-year budget risk; loss of funding would create a £0.737m pressure and would require service cuts or reserve drawdown to manage.
findings.figures: £0.737m grant dependency; potential pressure if removed or reduced
findings.quote: Currently waiting for confirmation from Welsh Government of the expected Sustainable Waste Management Grant 2025/2026 revenue grant funding... Concern is that WG will reduce or remove the funding due to the DEFRA (pEPR funding) from central government.

findings.headline: Homelessness presentations increased significantly after new eligibility category came into force
findings.detail: The 11th priority need category (at risk of rough sleeping) under Section 70 of the Housing (Wales) Act 2014 broadened eligibility and significantly increased the number of households presenting to the homelessness service. This structural change occurred in 2024/25 and the upward trend in presentations has continued through 2025/26 and into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Homelessness spending is material to council budgets. A structural increase in eligible households due to legislative change creates sustained demand pressure that is outside the council's control and requires budget provision.
findings.figures: Monthly figures in 2025/26 running higher than 2024/25 in almost every month; trend continuing into 2026/27
findings.quote: The introduction of the 11th priority need category (at risk of rough sleeping) under Section 70 of the Housing (Wales) Act 2014, which broadened eligibility and significantly increased the number of households presenting to the service. This upward trend has continued into the current financial year

findings.headline: Fleet decarbonisation capacity constrained: depot at full capacity, infrastructure investment needed to enable ULEV transition
findings.detail: Alltami depot is operating at full capacity with no expansion headroom (constrained by adjacent businesses and A494 trunk road). The council states that 'significant investment' is needed for electrical grid capacity and ULEV infrastructure, and that 'without financial investment, our ability to decarbonise fleet will be hindered'.
findings.matters: Constrained facility capacity to meet own decarbonisation commitments signals either deferred capital investment or regulatory pressure requiring future spending that is not yet funded.
findings.figures: Currently 12 ULEVs on fleet (exceeded target of 8). Depot at full operational capacity.
findings.quote: The Alltami depot is currently operating at full capacity in terms of available space and service provision, and expansion is constrained by adjacent businesses and the proximity of the A494 trunk road. Previous assessments have highlighted the need for significant investment to enable decarbonisation of the Council's fleet vehicles to enhance the site's electrical grid capacity and support the transition to Ultra Low Emission Vehicles (ULEVs). Without financial investment, our ability to decarbonise fleet will be hindered.

findings.paper_title: Council Plan End of Year Performance Reporting 2025/26
findings.headline: Highway maintenance backlog of £48m with annual funding gap of £3.74m against steady-state requirement
findings.detail: Council survey identified £48m backlog in highway maintenance. Steady-state funding need for carriageways alone is £5.24m per year, but allocation is £1.5m capital plus £0.225m revenue across the entire highway estate. Council notes investment 'has not [reached steady state] at any time in the last 10 years' and that network condition 'will naturally continue to deteriorate each year, without sufficient annual investment'.
findings.matters: Persistent underinvestment relative to asset life creates either future catch-up capital spending pressure or progressive asset degradation; for a lender, it signals either constrained capital plans or deteriorating asset quality.
findings.figures: Maintenance backlog: £48m. Annual steady-state need: £5.24m (carriageways). Allocated: £1.5m capital + £0.225m revenue.
findings.quote: the last survey report showed that the investment required to clear the backlog of maintenance works totalled £48m. Currently, the Council has an allocation of £1.5m capital funding and £0.225m revenue funding for highway maintenance. It needs to be recognised that the condition of the highway network will naturally continue to deteriorate each year, without sufficient annual investment.

findings.paper_title: Council Plan End of Year Performance Reporting 2025/26
findings.headline: Unearmarked reserves at 3.39% of budget—improved but remains low compared to other Welsh councils
findings.detail: Available unearmarked reserves stand at £13.457m (3.39% of budget). The council explicitly acknowledges this falls below peer levels: 'our overall funding remains low compared to other Welsh Councils'.
findings.matters: Below-peer reserves reduce financial flexibility to absorb demand or funding shocks; for a lender, thin buffers indicate reduced capacity to manage volatility without additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Unearmarked reserves: £13.457m (3.39% of budget)
findings.quote: The projected level of available unearmarked reserves was £13.457m which equates to 3.39% of the budget. This shows an improved position although our overall funding remains low compared to other Welsh Councils.

findings.paper_title: Council Plan End of Year Performance Reporting 2025/26
findings.headline: Projected budget overspend of £2.776m as of March 2026 monitoring
findings.detail: Despite a 'legal and balanced budget' approved in February for 2026/27, the March budget monitoring report projected a £2.776m overspend for 2025/26. The council attributes this to 'ongoing risk relating to increasing service demand and uncertainties over future national funding levels'.
findings.matters: Material variance signals either demand-driven spending growth or cost control slippage; for a lender, this tests whether the council can hold to its medium-term financial plans.
findings.figures: Projected overspend: £2.776m
findings.quote: The budget monitoring report presented to Cabinet in March, indicated a projected overspend of £2.776m.

findings.paper_title: Council Plan End of Year Performance Reporting 2025/26
findings.headline: Only strategic objective rated RED: homelessness service delivery failing on disabled adaptations due to recruitment and capacity issues
findings.detail: The homelessness service is the sole RED-rated objective. Disabled adaptations are severely delayed: medium adaptations average 180 days against a 122-day target, large adaptations 704 days against a 456-day target—both well above government guidelines. The council cites 'capacity issues and difficulties in recruiting new surveyors', compounded by legacy case completion. Relief outcomes also fall short at 33% against a 40% target.
findings.matters: A RED-rated strategic objective signals service delivery breakdown in a core housing function; for a lender, this indicates either spending control failure (if paying to fix it) or deteriorating resilience in a high-need area.
findings.figures: Medium adaptations: 180 days vs 122-day target. Large adaptations: 704 days vs 456-day target. Relief outcomes: 33% vs 40% target.
findings.quote: Timescales for delivery on medium and large disabled adaptations remain above the number of days recommended in Government guidelines. The team continues to have capacity issues and difficulties in recruiting new surveyors.

findings.headline: Legal and third-party costs £0.489m over budget, driven by court cases and external legal support
findings.detail: Children's Services Legal & Third Party budget is projecting £0.489m overspend. This includes £0.114m for external legal costs due to the number of cases going through courts, £0.271m client support and section 17 costs, and £0.104m Direct Payments.
findings.matters: Rising legal costs in children's services suggest increased complexity in safeguarding casework and may indicate systemic caseload or court involvement pressures.
findings.figures: £0.489m total overspend; external legal costs £0.114m; client support and section 17 £0.271m; Direct Payments £0.104m
findings.quote: There is a projected overspend of £0.114m for legal costs due to the number of cases going through the courts and some use of external support. Client support and section 17 costs are also projected to overspend by £0.271m and Direct Payments by £0.104m.

findings.headline: Unfunded operational vehicles in waste and recycling with escalating costs for fuel, insurance and maintenance
findings.detail: Out-of-scope vehicles and plant in waste and recycling were originally funded by external grant but the council has never been given revenue funding to operate them and they were never included in the original fleet contract. The council is now facing escalating costs for fuel, insurance, servicing, maintenance and repairs with no budget allocation.
findings.matters: Hidden or unfunded operational commitments indicate budget gaps that may not be fully visible in headline figures and could require emergency allocation or reserves use if costs continue.
findings.figures: £0.200m potential pressure flagged for out-of-scope vehicles and plant
findings.quote: Further £0.200m potential pressure for out-of-scope vehicles and plant in waste and recycling. These are vehicles and plant that were originally funded by external grant funding, but the service has never been given any revenue funding to operate them, and they were never in scope of the original fleet contract, which has created a pressure due to increased costs for fuel, insurance, servicing, maintenance, and repairs.

findings.headline: Waste and recycling pressures: £0.550m increase in disposal costs plus £0.500m shortfall in income targets
findings.detail: Wood and hazardous waste disposal costs have increased £0.550m due to market prices. Meanwhile, the council is £0.200m short on HRC trade waste income and £0.300m short on DIY household waste income after Members did not implement the full proposed charging scheme. Total Streetscene & Transportation overspend is £1.739m.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls suggest the council's charging assumptions do not match reality, and external cost inflation in waste disposal has no matching revenue offset, putting sustainable balance at risk.
findings.figures: Waste disposal costs +£0.550m; HRC waste income shortfall £0.200m; DIY waste income shortfall £0.300m; total Streetscene & Transportation overspend £1.739m
findings.quote: The majority of this pressure comes from recent increases in costs for the disposal of wood and hazardous waste of some £0.550m. Added to this is an increase in bulky waste disposal costs and demand £0.057m and residual waste tonnage £0.050m. There is a projected shortfall of £0.200m for HRC trade waste income due to lack of take-up from businesses and a further £0.300m shortfall for the underachievement of the DIY household waste income target following Member decision not to fully implement the proposed charging for DIY waste.

findings.headline: Out-of-county placements continuing to grow with explicit risk of further increases before year-end
findings.detail: The council is projecting £0.934m overspend on out-of-county children's placements and £0.751m on education placements. The report explicitly flags that new high-cost placements have been added at month 4 and states there is 'significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase as the budget monitoring cycle progresses.'
findings.matters: Out-of-county placements are paid from council reserves when they exceed budget. Escalating volume and explicit risk statements suggest this could be a larger budget pressure at year-end than currently forecast.
findings.figures: Out-of-county children's £0.934m; out-of-county education £0.751m; total out-of-county £1.685m
findings.quote: A number of new high-cost placements have been added to the current cohort at month 4, causing projected expenditure to exceed the approved budget. There is a significant risk that the projected overspend will continue to increase as the budget monitoring cycle progresses.

findings.headline: Children's Services agency staffing costs £0.772m over budget due to recruitment and retention challenges
findings.detail: The council is spending significantly above budget on temporary agency cover for social worker posts. It notes challenges recruiting and retaining staff and has started recruiting newly qualified social workers to reduce future agency reliance, but the cost pressure is live now.
findings.matters: Persistent agency spend signals operational stress in a statutory service and suggests permanent staffing investment may be needed, with implications for future budget sustainability.
findings.figures: £0.772m agency cost overspend in professional support (children's)
findings.quote: The professional support teams are projecting an overspend of £0.772m which is mainly caused by agency costs due to challenges recruiting and retaining social workers. Work has commenced to recruit newly qualified social workers to assist with reducing future reliance on agency staff.

findings.headline: Social services demand-led overspend of £4.390m, with Learning Disability care packages alone £2.194m over budget
findings.detail: The Learning Disability service is projecting £2.194m overspend from independent care provision, with additional £0.520m overspend in Physical Disability services. Older People homecare is £1.278m over budget due to reablement and hospital minimisation costs. These are structural demand pressures, not one-off items.
findings.matters: Demand-led social care overspends indicate the council's base budget does not match demographic need and may require reserve drawdown or borrowing to balance year-end.
findings.figures: £4.390m total social services overspend; Learning Disability £2.194m; Older People homecare £1.278m; PDSI £0.520m
findings.quote: The costs of care packages for independently provided services for the Learning Disability service is projecting an overspend of £2.194m which includes care provision through direct payments, supported living and residential services. The Physical Disability and Sensory Impairment (PDSI) is also projecting an overspend of £0.520m due to increased net costs of care packages.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: The one-off budget measures that balanced 2026/27 (Welsh Government windfall and pension gain) will not recur.
findings.detail: The council notes: "last year the Council benefited from a late Welsh Government additional budget agreement and a significant positive contribution from the triennial actuarial review of our pension contributions. This greatly assisted with enabling the Council to set a legal and balanced budget for the 2026/27 financial year and is unlikely to be available again."
findings.matters: This signals that 2026/27's balance was not structural. The council relied on windfalls to mask an underlying gap. It now faces that structural shortfall without cushion, making the 2027/28 position materially harder to resolve.
findings.figures: Pension and Welsh Government benefits not quantified.
findings.quote: last year the Council benefited from a late Welsh Government additional budget agreement and a significant positive contribution from the triennial actuarial review of our pension contributions. This greatly assisted with enabling the Council to set a legal and balanced budget for the 2026/27 financial year and is unlikely to be available again.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: The council is already overspending in the current year and will burn reserves to cover the deficit.
findings.detail: The council states: "Due to the significant projected overspend in the current financial year, any earmarked reserves that can be released will be required to improve the in-year position." Reserves are being consumed in 2026/27 before tackling the larger 2027/28 gap.
findings.matters: Reserve burn in the current year reduces the buffer available for 2027/28 pressures and future shocks. A lender tracking liquidity would be concerned that the council is consuming reserves to avoid structural action in the present, leaving fewer options for a projected larger shortfall.
findings.figures: Magnitude of current-year overspend not specified.
findings.quote: Due to the significant projected overspend in the current financial year, any earmarked reserves that can be released will be required to improve the in-year position.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: The council states it may fail to meet its statutory duty to set a legal and balanced budget.
findings.detail: The executive summary and conclusions warn: "Unless sufficient cost reductions are identified that are achievable and deliverable the Council will not meet its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget." The paper describes the position repeatedly as "serious and major."
findings.matters: A statutory budget-setting failure triggers Government intervention, potential administration, or special measures. For a lender, it signals the risk of emergency service cuts, emergency borrowing, or external control that could impair the council's ability to service debt.
findings.figures: None; governance statement.
findings.quote: Unless sufficient cost reductions are identified that are achievable and deliverable the Council will not meet its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: Cost reduction options are heavily weighted toward high-risk or unachievable cuts; only £1.8m of £10m in options are rated green.
findings.detail: Chief officers evaluated what a 10% portfolio cost reduction would require. Of the £10.019m identified: £3.555m rated 'Black' (highest risk), £3.042m 'Red', £1.597m 'Amber', and only £1.825m 'Green'. The council reports: "it has proven extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards."
findings.matters: A lender assessing refinance or facility renewal risk needs to know whether the council can credibly deliver identified savings. With 80% of cost reduction options carrying high delivery or quality-impact risk, the council lacks credible near-term savings headroom.
findings.figures: Cost reduction evaluation (10% exercise): Black £3.555m, Red £3.042m, Amber £1.597m, Green £1.825m; total £10.019m.
findings.quote: As expected, it has proven extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Budget 2027/28
findings.headline: The council faces an unfunded budget deficit of £16–25m in 2027/28 after a £27.866m additional requirement.
findings.detail: The council's total additional budget requirement is £27.866m. Even under the optimistic funding scenario (3–4% Welsh Government AEF uplift), this leaves a shortfall of £16.106m to £19.046m. The central planning assumption (2–3% uplift) leaves £19.046m to £21.986m unfunded. No scenario closes the gap without major action.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty that the council can balance its budget without unsustainable reserve drawdowns or service collapse. A £19–22m shortfall with limited identified solutions signals material budget-setting and liquidity risk.
findings.figures: Additional budget requirement £27.866m; scenario shortfalls: Optimistic (3–4% funding) £16.106m–£19.046m; Central (2–3%) £19.046m–£21.986m; Pessimistic (1–2%) £21.986m–£24.926m.
findings.quote: the Council would still need to identify a combination of additional income (including local taxation) and cost reductions in the region of £19.046m to £21.986m based on the central planning assumption.

findings.headline: £25m PWLB borrowing taken during 2025/26 to support long-term capital financing
findings.detail: Flintshire borrowed £25m from PWLB as part of its strategy to fix a portion of the long-term borrowing requirement. The council explored debt rescheduling options but found early repayment premiums uneconomic, so no rescheduling occurred.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing decisions and debt management choices are key indicators of the council's financial strategy and debt trajectory.
findings.quote: During the year, a total of £25m Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) loans were taken out to support the strategy of fixing a portion of the long-term borrowing requirement.

findings.headline: Flintshire's temporary accommodation demand increased by 26.6% in a year, the highest in North Wales and among the highest nationally
findings.detail: Flintshire's temporary accommodation caseload rose from 488 to 618 individuals between April 2025 and April 2026. The growth was continuous throughout the year, with numbers exceeding 600 by year-end. This contrasts sharply with the all-Wales reduction of 4.8% and even the North Wales regional increase of just 0.5%, indicating concentrated pressure in Flintshire.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory duty councils cannot refuse. A 26.6% annual surge in numbers represents an uncontrollable cost pressure; each additional person increases spending on emergency housing, support services, and staff. A finance director must budget for this; a lender assesses whether the council can absorb the cost without drawing reserves or cutting other services.
findings.figures: +130 individuals, +26.6%, from 488 to 618; homelessness rate 4.0 per 1,000 residents
findings.quote: Flintshire recorded the largest increase in the region, rising from 488 to 618 individuals (+130, +26.6%), and was one of the highest increases nationally.

findings.paper_title: Audit Wales Report on Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: Audit Wales found council cannot demonstrate value for money in temporary accommodation spending
findings.detail: Audit Wales findings state councils are 'spending considerable amounts of money on temporary accommodation which in many cases does not meet people's needs' and 'do not understand whether they are getting value for money from their temporary accommodation.'
findings.matters: An audit weakness in value-for-money assessment of a large discretionary service is a governance and efficiency concern; suggests inefficiency in deployment of significant resources
findings.figures: considerable amounts of money
findings.quote: Are spending considerable amounts of money on temporary accommodation which in many cases does not meet people's needs. Do not understand whether they are getting value for money from their temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Audit Wales Report on Temporary Accommodation
findings.headline: Service explicitly identified as significant financial risk with uncertain mitigation effectiveness
findings.detail: The council acknowledges homelessness as 'a significant financial risk should demand levels not start to fall' while admitting that 'the impact of the mitigations being put in place are difficult to predict.' This describes both current vulnerability and uncertainty about whether interventions will work.
findings.matters: An unresolved financial risk with uncertain remediation could lead to unplanned spending, supplementary budgets, or reserve draws
findings.figures: no figures
findings.quote: this area is still identified as a significant financial risk should demand levels not start to fall

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are creating budget pressures requiring specific financial modeling and monthly monitoring of emerging costs.
findings.detail: The council has conducted financial modeling to understand temporary and emergency accommodation costs, which informed the setting of a specific budget pressure amount for 2025/26. This financial modeling is monitored monthly to identify emerging pressures. The council is restructuring procurement from April 2027 to improve value for money.
findings.matters: Demand-driven service costs that require dedicated budget reserves and monthly monitoring for emerging pressures indicate structural financial challenges that consume council liquidity.
findings.figures: Budget pressure amount for 2025/26 (specific figure not stated)
findings.quote: This financial modelling informed the budget pressure amount required to in 2025/26. This financial modelling is monitored monthly to ensure any emerging pressures are identified and responded to.

findings.headline: £1.000m waste infrastructure capital deferred to 2027/28 pending completion of strategic review
findings.detail: Council's Resource and Waste Strategy review, adopted in March 2024, remains ongoing with outline business case due end of 2026/27. Capital expenditure on waste services infrastructure has been deferred until 2027/28, resulting in a 47% underspend (£1.000m) on waste services budget projected for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Material deferral of strategic infrastructure investment; finance director needs revised capital programme timeline; lender needs visibility on when waste capacity decisions and expenditure will occur to assess council's service provision capacity.
findings.figures: Waste Services budget £2.128m, projected outturn £1.128m (underspend £1.000m, representing -47% variance)
findings.quote: The review is ongoing and aims to deliver the outline business case by the end of the 2026/27 financial year.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs forecast to rise 290 basis points due to capital programme expansion
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs (interest and MRP) forecast to increase from 16.4% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 19.3% in 2026/27, with further increase to 19.7% in 2027/28. Rise is driven by HRA capital expenditure expansion including WHQS improvements (£11.033m), major works (£3.150m), and SHARP programme (£4.841m) funded through borrowing. Financing costs then stabilize at 19.7% from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: Material 290bp year-on-year increase puts HRA leverage approaching typical prudential limits. Lender needs to assess whether HRA revenue base can sustain these elevated financing costs long-term and whether HRA business model remains viable.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs 16.4% (2025/26 actual) rising to 19.3% (2026/27 forecast) and 19.7% (2027/28 estimate)
findings.quote: The increase in estimated CFR between 2025/26 and 2026/27 is estimated expenditure for the HRA and NEW Homes, Supported Borrowing, and Council Fund schemes including the Sustainable Communities for Schools programme and LGBI for Highways.

findings.headline: After over a decade of austerity, the council has exhausted most low-cost savings options and faces very difficult choices ahead
findings.detail: The council repeatedly emphasizes that the historic scale of cost reductions already taken across portfolios during austerity "leaves very limited options of scale for further cost reductions." Further reductions will require difficult choices with service impact.
findings.matters: This structural constraint means future budget gaps cannot be solved through incremental efficiency gains; they require material service cuts or tax increases
findings.figures: Over a decade of underfunding and cost reductions across all portfolios
findings.quote: As repeatedly reported, the scale of historic cost reductions already taken from portfolios during the period of austerity and beyond leaves very limited options of scale for further cost reductions and some very difficult choices will need to be made.

findings.headline: No official Welsh Government settlement for 2027/28 has been announced; budget planning is based on uncertain assumptions
findings.detail: The council is operating on three funding scenarios (pessimistic 1–2%, central 2–3%, optimistic 3–4% uplift) pending the official Welsh Government draft budget in mid-November. Each 1% uplift equals £2.940m. Current planning uses central case but carries material settlement risk.
findings.matters: Final budget position could shift materially once the settlement is known; worst-case scenario is 1% uplift delivering only £2.9m against a £27.9m requirement
findings.figures: 1% uplift = £2.940m; pessimistic scenario £2.940m–£5.880m; central £5.880m–£8.820m; optimistic £8.820m–£11.760m
findings.quote: At this stage, there is no official Welsh local government settlement for 2027/28 so all that we can do is base our assumptions on any potential implications from UK Spending Reviews and an assessment of the resulting outlook for the overall Welsh Government budget.

findings.headline: The council may not meet its statutory obligation to set a balanced budget by March 2027 if cost reductions prove insufficient
findings.detail: The document repeatedly warns that unless sufficient achievable and deliverable cost reductions are identified, the council will breach its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget. This is stated as a direct risk, not a hypothetical.
findings.matters: Failure to set a balanced budget is a governance failure that could trigger Welsh Government intervention, external administration, or use of extraordinary powers
findings.figures: Legal budget deadline: March 2027
findings.quote: Unless sufficient cost reductions are identified that are achievable and deliverable the Council will not meet its statutory obligation to set a legal and balanced budget.

findings.headline: Of £10m in evaluated cost reductions across all portfolios, only £1.8m (18%) are rated low-risk; most carry high risk to service quality
findings.detail: When the council evaluated a 10% cost reduction exercise across portfolios, results were: Black (highest risk) £3.555m; Red £3.042m; Amber £1.597m; Green (lowest risk) £1.825m. The council explicitly notes it has proven "extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards."
findings.matters: Limited low-risk options means the council will be forced to implement high-risk cuts with direct impact on service provision, affecting both operational resilience and council income
findings.figures: Green (low-risk): £1.825m; Amber: £1.597m; Red: £3.042m; Black (highest-risk): £3.555m; total £10.019m
findings.quote: As expected, it has proven extremely difficult to identify areas that won't impact on service quality and standards.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 balanced budget relied on non-recurring Welsh Government funding and pension contribution relief that will not repeat
findings.detail: Last year the council benefited from a late Welsh Government budget agreement and a significant positive contribution from a triennial pension actuarial review. Both are explicitly described as unlikely to be available again, meaning 2027/28 cannot rely on these tailwinds.
findings.matters: This explains why the 2027/28 position is materially worse despite similar stated budget pressures, and shows the previous year's balance was not structural
findings.figures: 2026/27 benefited from 4.5% uplift following additional negotiations
findings.quote: This greatly assisted with enabling the Council to set a legal and balanced budget for the 2026/27 financial year and is unlikely to be available again.

findings.headline: The council is projecting a significant overspend in 2026/27 and plans to draw down earmarked reserves to cover it
findings.detail: The document states that due to a projected overspend in the current financial year, the council will release available earmarked reserves to improve the in-year position. It warns that using reserves to balance the budget should only occur for one-off or time-limited costs, not for structural deficits.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover operational deficits in the current year signals worsening cash position and reduces the buffer available for future shocks
findings.figures: No specific reserve figure disclosed; draws occurring in 2026/27
findings.quote: Due to the significant projected overspend in the current financial year, any earmarked reserves that can be released will be required to improve the in-year position.

findings.headline: The council faces a £19–22m structural budget gap for 2027/28 under central funding assumptions
findings.detail: Flintshire identified an additional budget requirement of £27.866m for 2027/28. Under central planning assumptions (2–3% funding uplift from Welsh Government), this leaves a shortfall of £19.046m to £21.986m. Even under optimistic scenarios (3–4% uplift), the gap remains £16–19m. The council must find solutions through cost reductions and increased income to set a legal and balanced budget.
findings.matters: A structural gap of this magnitude indicates the council cannot sustain current service levels without major reductions; it signals material pressure on financial sustainability for a borrower
findings.figures: £27.866m additional budget requirement; £19.046m–£21.986m shortfall (central scenario); £16.106m–£19.046m shortfall (optimistic scenario)
findings.quote: If the analysis above is an accurate reflection of the likely Welsh Government settlement, the Council would still need to identify a combination of additional income (including local taxation) and cost reductions in the region of £19.046m to £21.986m based on the central planning assumption.

findings.headline: Reserves rated Amber (score 9), flagged as a material risk requiring mitigation
findings.detail: The council classifies reserve adequacy as an Amber risk at 9 out of 25, indicating it judges reserves insufficient for its identified risks. The score has not changed from the previous quarter.
findings.matters: Reserves function as the council's financial buffer against revenue shocks; an Amber rating signals limited financial flexibility in a period of MTFS and schools stress.
findings.figures: Risk Score 9 out of 25
findings.quote: RCF01 – Reserves – Risk Score 9 (Same, previously 9)

findings.headline: Financial viability of schools is rated Red at score 25, the highest risk on the corporate register
findings.detail: Schools financial viability is the single highest-rated risk at 25 out of 25 and has not improved. Schools represent a material delegated budget; financial distress there cascades into council-wide sustainability issues and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Schools absorb a large share of council spending; financial difficulties in delegated budgets force the council into additional spending or borrowing.
findings.figures: Risk Score 25 out of 25; highest risk on register
findings.quote: REY01 - Financial Viability of Schools – Risk Score 25 (Same, previously 25)

findings.headline: Medium-term Financial Strategy rated Red (score 20 out of 25), unchanged from previous quarter
findings.detail: The MTFS remains at the council's second-highest risk level with no improvement made. This indicates material challenges in the council's ability to balance its budget over the medium term, a core concern for service continuity.
